question: A pulse travels along a heavy rope and reaches a knot where the rope becomes a light thread; the tension is the same throughout. A second, identical pulse travels along the same heavy rope toward a wall. Which pair of reflections do you see?

answers.answer: Upright off the light thread, inverted off the wall.
answers.feedback: Right, and one formula covers both. The reflected amplitude is r = (Z1 - Z2)/(Z1 + Z2) with Z = sqrt(T mu), so the sign of r is the sign of Z1 - Z2: the echo inverts only when the far side is *harder* than the near one. A light thread has a smaller Z, so r > 0 and the pulse returns upright; a wall is the limit Z2 -> infinity, so r = -1 and the pulse returns upside down. Simulated, the same junction gives +1/3 from the heavy side and -1/3 from the light side of a 4:1 density pair, with the change of sign exactly at equal densities.

answers.answer: Inverted in both cases, since reflection always flips a pulse.
answers.feedback: This is the module's misconception, and it comes from meeting reflection first at a wall, which is one end of the range rather than the rule. Run the formula: r = (Z1 - Z2)/(Z1 + Z2) is negative only for Z2 > Z1. Onto a lighter medium r is positive and the echo is upright — measured at +0.6669 for a 25:1 density drop, against +2/3 predicted. The wall is the special case, not the general one, and the general case turns over at the match rather than at some threshold of hardness.

answers.answer: Upright in both cases, since the string is continuous through the knot and cannot flip.
answers.feedback: Continuity of the string is one of the two junction conditions, and it gives 1 + r = t — it does not fix the sign of r on its own. The other condition, that the massless joint carries no net force, is what produces r = (Z1 - Z2)/(Z1 + Z2). At a wall the displacement must stay zero at all times, which forces the returning pulse to cancel the incoming one point by point: that is exactly an inverted copy.

answers.answer: Inverted off the light thread, upright off the wall.
answers.feedback: This has the two cases exactly swapped. The useful mental image is what the far side does back to the string. A wall cannot move, so it pulls back with whatever force is needed, and that reaction is the inverted pulse leaving. A thread offers almost no resistance, so the end flies up — nearly twice as far as the incident pulse alone would take it — and the echo it launches is upright.

question: A string with mu1 = 4.0 g/m is joined to one with mu2 = 36 g/m under a common tension. A wave arrives from the light side. What is the transmitted displacement amplitude coefficient t?

answers.feedback: Impedances first: Z = sqrt(T mu), so Z2/Z1 = sqrt(36/4.0) = 3 whatever the tension is — the tension cancels out of every coefficient at a junction, because it is one number for both sides. Then t = 2 Z1/(Z1 + Z2) = 2/(1 + 3) = 0.5 and r = (1 - 3)/(1 + 3) = -0.5. Check with 1 + r = t: 1 - 0.5 = 0.5. The transmitted wave is half the height of the incident one and the echo is inverted at half its height, which does *not* mean half the energy goes each way — see the power coefficients, where R = 0.25 and T = 0.75.

question: A pulse crosses from a string onto one a hundred times lighter. The transmitted pulse is 1.82 times taller than the incident pulse. What happened to the energy?

answers.answer: Most of it reflected. The light string is cheap to move, so a large motion of it carries little power — the transmitted fraction is 0.33 and the reflected 0.67.
answers.feedback: Right. Power is (1/2) Z (omega A)^2, so the transmitted power carries the far side's impedance, not the near side's: T = (Z2/Z1) t^2. Here Z2/Z1 = 1/10 and t = 1.818, so T = 0.1 x 3.31 = 0.331, and R = r^2 = 0.818^2 = 0.669. They sum to 1, as they must. A large amplitude on a medium that is cheap to move is not much energy — the same reason a loudspeaker cone moves far in air and hardly at all in water.

answers.answer: Energy was gained at the junction, because the far string adds its own motion to the wave.
answers.feedback: Nothing at the junction can add energy: the joint is massless, lossless and carries no store of its own. R + T = 1 follows from the two matching conditions by algebra — substitute r and t and the numerators (Z1 - Z2)^2 + 4 Z1 Z2 collapse onto (Z1 + Z2)^2 — so the bookkeeping was fixed before any energy question was asked. What changed at the junction is the *price* of a given amplitude, not the total.

answers.answer: The energy split evenly, since amplitude 1.82 and amplitude 0.82 are close to equal shares.
answers.feedback: Amplitudes are not energies, and the two do not even go in the same order here: the taller pulse is the weaker one. Squaring the amplitudes is not enough either, because the two pulses live on different media. The transmitted fraction needs the flux factor Z2/Z1 in front of t^2, and it is that factor — one tenth here — that turns a squared amplitude ratio of 3.31 into a power fraction of 0.33.

answers.answer: It is stored at the junction and released slowly afterwards.
answers.feedback: A massless, lossless joint has nowhere to store anything and no time constant with which to release it. Simulating the run and weighing both sides after the pulses separate gives R + T = 1 to seven decimal places, with no residue sitting at the junction. A junction that did store energy would be a different model — a bead of finite mass at the joint, which is a good exam question and not this one.

question: Two strings under common tension have densities in the ratio mu2/mu1 = 9. What fraction of an incident wave's energy is transmitted across the junction? Give T as a decimal.

answers.feedback: Z2/Z1 = sqrt(9) = 3, so r = (1 - 3)/(1 + 3) = -0.5 and t = 2/(1 + 3) = 0.5. Then R = r^2 = 0.25 and T = (Z2/Z1) t^2 = 3 x 0.25 = 0.75, which sum to 1. Two traps to avoid. T is not t^2 = 0.25: the transmitted wave travels on the other medium, and the flux factor Z2/Z1 has to come with it. And T is not 1 - t = 0.5: a fraction of energy is never one minus a fraction of amplitude. Note that the answer is the same if the wave arrives from the heavy side instead, where r = +0.5 and t = 1.5 — different amplitudes, identical energy split.

question: Which junction between two media produces no reflection at all?

answers.answer: One where the two impedances are equal, whatever the individual material constants are.
answers.feedback: Right: r = 0 requires exactly Z1 = Z2 and nothing else. The individual constants may differ — a fluid's density and sound speed, or a cable's inductance and capacitance per metre, can both change as long as the product that makes Z comes out the same. On a *string* this is a blunt instrument, because tension is one number from end to end, so equal impedance means equal density and the matched junction is a string with no junction in it. Matching two media that are both given takes an intermediate layer — the quarter-wave section of the advanced section.

answers.answer: One where the two wave speeds are equal.
answers.feedback: Equal speeds are neither necessary nor sufficient. Z = sqrt(T mu) and v = sqrt(T/mu) are independent combinations of the same two constants, so two media can share a speed and differ in impedance — and then a wave crosses without changing wavelength and still reflects. On a string with one tension the two happen to travel together, which is why this answer feels right and stops being right the moment the tension is allowed to differ, as it does for sound in two different fluids.

answers.answer: One where the two densities are equal, since equal mass per metre means nothing changes.
answers.feedback: True on a string under uniform tension, and only there — which makes it a fact about this apparatus rather than the criterion. The criterion is on Z. Ultrasound gel is matched to tissue while being a completely different material; a 50 ohm resistor terminates a 50 ohm cable while being neither a cable nor a wave-carrying medium at all.

answers.answer: Any junction, provided the wave arrives slowly enough that the second medium has time to respond.
answers.feedback: There is no such threshold: r and t contain no frequency at all, so a mismatched junction reflects the same fraction at every frequency. What *can* depend on frequency is a junction that is not a point — a density that changes gradually over a distance comparable with the wavelength reflects less and less as the ramp widens, which is the problem set's smeared junction and the reason a tsunami grows instead of bouncing.

question: Ultrasound gel has an acoustic impedance close to that of soft tissue (about 1.6e6 against 1.5e6 kg m^-2 s^-1); air's is about 430. What does the gel accomplish?

answers.answer: It replaces the air gap, whose enormous impedance mismatch with tissue would reflect essentially all of the sound.
answers.feedback: Right, and the numbers are dramatic. For a tissue-air interface, r = (1.5e6 - 430)/(1.5e6 + 430) = 0.9994, so R = 0.9989: about 99.9% of the sound comes straight back and the image is black, not merely dim. With gel in the gap, Z2/Z1 = 1.6/1.5 gives r = -0.032 and R = 0.001 — one part in a thousand reflected. The gel is not a lubricant and conducts sound no better than tissue does; it is there to be nearly the same impedance as what is on both sides of it.

answers.answer: It lubricates the probe so that the transducer can be moved smoothly across the skin.
answers.feedback: It does do that, and it is not why the image fails without it. A dry probe pressed firmly still leaves a microscopic air layer, and the tissue-air mismatch reflects about 99.9% of the sound at that layer. Reflectance depends on the impedance ratio and not at all on friction: R = ((Z1 - Z2)/(Z1 + Z2))^2 = 0.9989 for tissue against air.

answers.answer: It slows the sound down so that more of it can be transmitted into the body.
answers.feedback: Nothing in r or t depends on the speed by itself. The coefficients contain the impedances only, Z = rho c, and a medium can be made slower without changing Z at all — raise rho and lower c in proportion. The gel works by matching the product, not by changing either factor in a particular direction.

answers.answer: It absorbs the reflected sound so that it does not re-enter the probe and confuse the image.
answers.feedback: The gel is very nearly lossless at these frequencies over a fraction of a millimetre — it absorbs almost nothing. It also does not need to: matching means the reflection is never created, rather than created and then mopped up. That distinction matters, since absorbing the echo would cost the same energy the image needs, while matching keeps it and sends it into the patient.
